title: Lakshmana's line
hookLine: a line in the dust, a holy man at the door, and a sacred duty turned into a trap
carry: maryada: the guest is god, the line holds
tomorrow: the holy man is Ravana. who tries to stop him?
last: VIVEKA: TELLING THE REAL FROM THE FAKE.

lines: A HOLY MAN AT THE EDGE.
cards: Before Lakshmana leaves, in a later telling of the story, he does one last thing. With an arrow, he draws a line in the dust all the way around the hut.
Stay inside this line, he tells Sita, whatever happens, whoever comes. Nothing evil can cross it. Then he runs into the forest.
The clearing goes quiet. A few minutes later, a holy man walks out of the trees: an old wandering ascetic with a staff and a begging bowl, chanting softly. He stops at the edge of the line.
And, very politely, he asks for food.

teach.b: The holy man is Ravana in disguise. In that telling, he can't cross the line, so he needs Sita to cross it. He asks for alms.
She offers them from inside. He says: a holy man can't take food from someone behind a barrier. Come out and give it properly, or I'll leave, and you'll have turned away a guest.

teach.h: ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS GOD.
teach.b: That's the trap, and it's built from a real Hindu teaching: atithi devo bhava, treat the guest as God. Feeding whoever comes to the door is a sacred duty, and Sita was raised on it. So she lifts her foot and steps over.
One thing, plainly: the line isn't in Valmiki's Ramayana. In Valmiki, Lakshmana just leaves, and Sita welcomes the disguised Ravana as a guest, with water and food.

teach.h: NOT IN VALMIKI. IT GREW LATER.
teach.b: The line grew in later retellings, and it became a phrase: a Lakshmana rekha is a limit you must not cross.

teach.h: MARYADA: THE LIMIT OF RIGHT CONDUCT.
teach.b: Hindus have an older word for that kind of limit: maryada, the boundary of right conduct. It's why Rama is called Maryada Purushottam, the best of men, who keeps every limit.

teach.h: THE GUEST IS GOD. THE LINE HOLDS.
teach.b: The story holds both teachings at once. The guest is God; Hindu homes still feed whoever comes. And a sacred duty can be borrowed by someone who means harm.
Ravana didn't break Sita's goodness. He used it. Maryada is the line that keeps your kindness your own.
In a family, at a job, with a friend who knows exactly which kind word will make you bend, it's the same question: is this generosity, or is someone using it?

how: In everyday speech across India, a Lakshmana rekha is a boundary that must not be crossed, and Rama is called Maryada Purushottam, the one who keeps every limit; many Hindu homes still treat the guest as God, and the line around the hut is a well-known Ramlila moment though it is not in Valmiki.

o: a line in the dust: a limit not to cross
a vow Lakshmana took to guard his brother
the arrow Lakshmana carried into the forest

games.q: match the story to the teaching.

s: the Lakshmana rekha is in Valmiki's Ramayana
it appears in later retellings; in Valmiki, Lakshmana simply leaves.
Lakshmana rekha is an everyday phrase in India today
a limit you must not cross, in families, politics and friendships.
Sita crosses the line out of carelessness
she crosses out of a sacred duty, the guest treated as God, which Ravana uses against her.

games.q: your cousin is always welcome at your house. now he wants you to lie to his parents for him: 'family helps family.' what fits today's teaching?
o: family is family, so you lie for him.
keep the welcome and hold the line: you'll feed him, not lie for him.
games.why: atithi devo bhava and maryada together: the welcome is sacred, and so is the limit. Ravana used Sita's goodness; maryada keeps yours your own.

practice: Many Hindu homes still cook a little extra for whoever might come to the door. Picture your own door, and someone you'd feed gladly.
Then picture your line: one thing you won't do, even for someone polite, even when crossing would look kind. Say it once, quietly, the way Lakshmana drew his in the dust.

wordCard.voice: Lakshmana rekha. Lakshmana's line: drawn around the hut in later tellings, and now an everyday phrase for a limit you must not cross.

orig.note: Hindi, from Sanskrit: Lakshmana's line (rekha), a boundary not to be crossed.

carryVoice: Take this with you: maryada. The guest is God, and the line holds. Day fifty-one, done.
